newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND--US 97 corporate bond issuance seen strong.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND--US 97 corporate bond issuance seen strong.

text.p: New issues on the U.S. corporate bond market are surging past 1993's record volume of $286 billion this year, and analysts are predicting another stellar performance in 1997.
If interest rates stay at current levels, "we should see a lot of new corporate supply as interest rates are used as a guage for issuance," one high-grade syndicate source said.
"The fourth quarter is shaping into a tremendous quarter, and I'm sure what doesn't get done by the end of this year will certainly come back in the first quarter," he added.

The new issue calendar for 1997 is already building, as Italy prepares a $1.0 billion 10-year global debt deal and State Development Bank of China readies its $300 million 10-year Yankee debt offering, syndicate sources said.

As for 1996, research firm Securities Data Co reported that corporate debt issuance was approaching $290 billion. A sharp drop in U.S. Treasury yields triggered the avalanche of debt offerings as U.S. corporations took advantage of lower financing costs, syndicate managers said.
Securities Data said $30 billion in new high-yield bonds have been issued in 1996, putting junk bonds on track for their highest levels since 1993. Analysts expect that trend to continue too.

"We see good (high-yield) supply going forward driven by attractive rates; driven by continued economic activity here in the U.S., as well as abroad, and driven by a lot of cash in the high-yield market," said Art Penn, Head of Capital Markets at BT Securities Corp.
Pension fund money flowing into junk bonds gave the high-yield sector an added boost this year, analysts said.

"To a certain extent, the money coming in from pension funds has certainly been the little extra boost that this (high-yield) market needed," said Alan Ginsberg, director of high-yield and emerging debt at Smith Barney Inc.
"If fund flows start to slow down, typically issuance will also slow down, so I think we'll remain pretty much in balance" in the new year, Ginsberg added.

Corporate bond syndicate officials said AMG Data Services Inc reported $600 million in new cash poured into high-yield mutual funds in the week ended December 12. AMG official Robert Adler declined to comment on the figure.

In another high-yield market record, the 144A private placement market outpaced public offerings in 1996. Through the week of December 6, the market financed about $32.8 billion in 144A private placement debt offerings via 199 deals, compared with about $29.7 billion in public high-yield debt offerings via 135 deals, Merrill Lynch & Co said.
In 1997, "The 144A market will be as strong as it was in 1996," predicted BT Securities' Penn.

"We see no incremental premium that issuers would need to pay for in a 144A (offering), versus a publicly registered security," Penn said. "Therefore, the ease of being able to come to market quickly without a SEC review, and without waiting, will far outweigh any negatives."
Combined, public and private sector high-yield issuance, totaled $68.3 bilion through last week, nearing 1993's record level of $73.3 billion, according to Securities Data.
Analysts noted that the latest 12-month moving average on junk bond default rates is less than 2.0 percent, well under its 20-year average of 4.0 percent.

"With 1995's default rate at 3.2 percent we've actually gone lower and that helps to explain why we're observing this narrowing in yield spreads," said John Lonski, senior economist at Moody's Investors Service Inc.

In addition to the 1996 junk bond default rate being down from 1995, Lonski noted, it is also far below 1991's 10.5 percent peak rate as well as 1988's 3.6 percent, 1989's 5.8 percent and 1990's 8.7 percent.
"I do not think that a wide spread erosion of credit worth will impede corporate bond issuance in either the investment grade or high-yield markets," Lonski said.
"The issuance environment is quite attractive because current long-term investment grade corporate bond yields lag the last four years average by a relatively ample 25-30 basis points," Lonski said.
Lonski noted that with a four-year average of 7.85 percent for a single-A corporate credit "you're still about 30 basis points under the average with yields at 7.56 percent."

"I wouldn't begin to worry about issuance being trimmed by what are judged to be higher than trend, or above average corporate yields until we have (yields) move up by another 30 basis points or so," Lonski added.
He said new issues could start to slow, however, "once bond yields, as I believe they will, go back up above 7.0 percent beginning in the spring and into the summer of 1997.
So far this year, approximately $268 billion in new investment grade debt was priced in the corporate bond market, according to Securities Data.

"There's been more shelf registrations the first 11 months of the year than gross bond issuance, which suggest the potential for a strong year for corporate bond issuance is very much there," Lonski said.
"What matters is whether or not the interest rate environment is deemed favorable," he added.
